# Synthesis Principles {.unnumbered}

Parts I through VI developed the responsibilities needed to carry a task from a model proposal to an assessed outcome. They priced calls and candidate selection, separated information from derived computation, mediated effects and disclosures, and governed continuation, recovery, and evaluation. Learning and delegation introduced optional ways to change the system, each requiring evidence that the change serves the task. Part VII brings these responsibilities together on one incident-remediation trajectory. A working component is not enough: its assumptions must match the evidence, authority, and state supplied across the next boundary.

The synthesis returns to invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}) and the principles that refine it. Each transition needs an owner, a record, and a stated response when the available evidence is insufficient. These contracts also require someone authorized to adopt them. Assistance with writing a specification is different from authority to make it govern the task.

::: {#pri-vol3-specification-boundary .callout-principle title="The specification boundary"}

**Invariant**: A model can help formulate goals, propose designs, draft tests, and critique a task contract. Those outputs remain proposals: they do not independently adopt the contract, grant permission, change acceptance criteria, or certify the model's own work. Authorized people and organizations own those decisions and the residual duties they leave. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-conclusion-brooks.

**Implication**: Record which contract governs the task, who may authorize changes, what evidence supports acceptance, and who owns unresolved outcomes and continuing obligations. Evaluate generated specifications and checks against the intended requirements rather than treating consistency between a candidate and its own tests as sufficient evidence.

:::

@Sec-vol3-conclusion traces one incident through diagnostic reads, a scoped approval, an uncertain external effect, and an acceptance decision. It uses the contract to assign responsibility at subsystem boundaries, compares interventions using evidence, and constructs a scoped safety case. The closing argument concerns accountability rather than a limit on what assistance a model can provide: useful proposals still need authorized adoption, justified acceptance, and ownership of what remains unresolved.
